passages.t: When the wicked rule, the people groan
passages.happening:
‘A man who remains stiff-necked after much reproof will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery’ (verse 1). “When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan” (verse 2). ‘A man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father’ (verse 3).

‘By justice a king brings stability to the land, but a man who exacts tribute demolishes it’ (verse 4). ‘A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet’ (verse 5).

‘The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns’ (verse 7). ‘Mockers inflame a city, but the wise turn away anger’ (verse 8). A wise man who goes to court with a fool gets only raving and laughter (verse 9). ‘A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 29 closes the collection copied by Hezekiah's men. Like chapter 28, it looks at what happens to a people when the righteous or the wicked hold power, and how a ruler's justice or corruption sets the tone for a whole land.

Verse 4 sets a just king beside a man who exacts tribute, or, as some translate, a man of bribes or heavy levies. Israel's own history showed both. Solomon's heavy labor and taxes led the northern tribes to reject his son Rehoboam, and the kingdom split. Hezekiah's scribes lived with that legacy.

Verse 7 makes caring about the poor a mark of the righteous. The wicked do not even know the poor have a case.
passages.later: The northern tribes said to Rehoboam, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us” (1 Kings 12:4). And a psalm of Solomon prays for the king verse 4 describes: ‘May he vindicate the afflicted among the people; may he save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor’ (Psalm 72:4).
passages.asks: The righteous know the cause of the poor. Ask whether you know the real situation of the poor near you, or only opinions about them. And ask where you could turn anger away this week instead of feeding it.

passages.t: Light for every eye, and no vision
passages.happening:
‘If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked’ (verse 12). “The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both” (verse 13). A king who judges the poor fairly will have his throne established forever (verse 14).

‘A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother’ (verse 15). ‘Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul’ (verse 17).

Then a much-quoted saying: “Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint; but blessed is he who keeps the Law” (verse 18). A servant is not corrected by words alone (verse 19). ‘Do you see a man who speaks in haste? There is more hope for a fool than for him’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Verse 13 is like 22:2. The poor man and his oppressor both see by the same light, and God gives it to both.

Verse 14 echoes God's promise to David of a throne that would last. Kings across the ancient world boasted in their inscriptions of protecting the weak, so just rule was a shared ideal, even when it was rarely practiced.

Verses 15 and 17 belong with the other sayings on correcting children (13:24; 22:15; 23:13-14). Faithful parents read the rod in two ways: as measured physical discipline given calmly and in love, or as a picture of firm correction in general. The site's notes on those verses set out both, and take no side. Both readings agree that the aim is the child's good, that correction in anger or that injures is not discipline at all, and that nothing here gives anyone a warrant to harm a child. Verse 17's promise of rest describes the usual fruit of faithful correction, not a guarantee.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Households included servants, some of them bound by debt. Verses 19 and 21 reflect the social order of their day without endorsing every part of it.
passages.later: The prophet Amos warned of the famine verse 18 describes: ‘not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD’ (Amos 8:11). And the psalm says of the one who keeps the law, ‘Blessed are those who keep His testimonies and seek Him with all their heart’ (Psalm 119:2).
passages.hard:
Does verse 18 mean that people die without a vision for the future?

An older English translation, which says that without vision the people perish, is often quoted to support visionary leadership, goal-setting or planning. Those are not bad things, but they are not what the verse means.

The Hebrew word for vision, chazon, refers to revelation from God, the kind given to prophets. The verb means to cast off restraint, to run wild, more than to perish. And the verse's second half makes the point clear: ‘blessed is he who keeps the Law’ (verse 18).

So the proverb teaches that when God's word is absent or ignored, a people loses its moral bearings, and that the one who keeps God's instruction is the one who does well. Like all proverbs, it describes a pattern, not a mechanical guarantee. Its subject is revelation, not ambition.
passages.asks: Without God's word, a people runs wild. Ask how much of God's word is shaping your days, and what is shaping them instead. And ask whether you speak in haste, since verse 20 puts the hasty speaker below the fool.

passages.t: The fear of man, and justice from the LORD
passages.happening:
‘An angry man stirs up dissension, and a hot-tempered man abounds in transgression’ (verse 22). ‘A man’s pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor’ (verse 23). A thief's partner who hears the public oath and says nothing hates his own soul (verse 24).

“The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high” (verse 25). ‘Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD’ (verse 26).

The collection ends with the two ways: ‘An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Verse 24 refers to a legal custom. When a crime was committed, a public charge or oath was pronounced on anyone who knew something and did not testify. A thief's partner who hears it and stays silent brings guilt on himself.

Petitioners at a royal court had to win access to the king for their case to be heard. Verse 26 says the justice that finally counts comes from the LORD.

The last verse closes the whole collection. The two ways that run through Proverbs are so opposed that each finds the other intolerable.
passages.later: The law behind verse 24: ‘If someone sins by failing to testify when he hears a public charge about something he has witnessed, whether he has seen it or learned of it, he shall bear the iniquity’ (Leviticus 5:1). And the psalm says what verse 25 says: ‘It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man’ (Psalm 118:8).
passages.asks: The fear of man is a snare. Ask whose approval you are most afraid of losing, and what it has cost you. And ask what it would look like to trust the LORD in that place instead.
